theme: When I am afraid I trust in you
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 56 and Psalm 57. Both come from David’s fugitive years. Notice the repeated refrains and the confidence they reflect.
settingTheScene: Psalm 56 is set “when the Philistines seized him in Gath,” and Psalm 57 “when he fled from Saul, in the cave.” Both carry the title Miktam, and both use the tune “Do Not Destroy.” They are written in the narrowest places: a foreign city and a cave. Both end in a refrain of praise, which shows that faith can speak boldly even when circumstances are small and frightening.
observation: “When I am afraid, I put my trust in you” (56:3).
“In God, whose word I praise, in God I trust; I shall not be afraid. What can flesh do to me?” (56:4).
“You have kept count of my tossings; put my tears in your bottle. Are they not in your book?” (56:8).
“This I know, that God is for me” (56:9).
“Be merciful to me, O God, be merciful to me, for in you my soul takes refuge; in the shadow of your wings I will take refuge, till the storms of destruction pass by” (57:1).
“I cry out to God Most High, to God who fulfills his purpose for me” (57:2).
“My heart is steadfast, O God, my heart is steadfast! I will sing and make melody!” (57:7).
“Be exalted, O God, above the heavens! Let your glory be over all the earth!” (57:5, 11).
interpretation:
Psalm 56 gives a very honest account of fear. “When I am afraid.” It does not say “if.” David is afraid. He is in Gath, the home of Goliath, with the sword of Goliath in his hand. The psalm says that fear is a normal part of life, and the answer is not to deny it, but to bring it to God. “When I am afraid, I put my trust in you.” Courage in the Bible is not the absence of fear. It is trust in the midst of it.

The image of God collecting tears in a bottle has been loved for centuries. God does not just see our sorrow. He keeps count of our tossings and records our tears. Nothing is wasted. No tear falls unnoticed. It is among the most tender images in the Psalms.

And verse 9: “This I know, that God is for me.” It is a statement of settled conviction. It is the truth David holds to when he cannot see anything else. Paul would later write, “If God is for us, who can be against us?” (Romans 8:31).

Psalm 57 is set in a cave, but the cave becomes a place of high praise. “In the shadow of your wings I will take refuge, till the storms of destruction pass by.” It is a refuge for a season. David knows that the storm will pass. His confidence rests on God, “who fulfills his purpose for me.” God has a plan, and the cave cannot stop it.

The two refrains are lovely. Psalm 56 says, “In God I trust; I shall not be afraid.” Psalm 57 says, “Be exalted, O God, above the heavens!” In the first, trust is the response to fear. In the second, praise is the response to danger. Both turn the heart from circumstances to God.

Verse 8 of Psalm 57 is a morning song: “Awake, my glory! Awake, O harp and lyre! I will awake the dawn!” David wakes the dawn, rather than waiting for it.
connection: Jesus found refuge not in a cave but in his Father, who “collects” his tears (Hebrews 5:7). Paul quotes Psalm 56:4 in spirit in Romans 8:31 and Hebrews 13:6. Psalm 57:10 (“your steadfast love is great to the heavens”) echoes in Ephesians 3:18-19. Jesus said, “In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world” (John 16:33).
application:
Pray, “When I am afraid, I put my trust in you,” the next time you feel fear rising.

Remember that God keeps your tears in a bottle. None of them is wasted.

Wake the dawn with praise tomorrow morning, even if it is hard.
prayerPrompts: Tell God what makes you afraid, and say, “I trust you.”
Thank him that he keeps count of your tears.
Ask him to be exalted above your fears.
